extracted.intended_audience: patent drafters, patent attorneys, patent agents (practitioners prosecuting patent applications)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for drafting responses, amending applications, conducting interviews, appeals, divisional/continuation practice, oppositions and issuance formalities during patent prosecution across multiple jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond fully to all examiner comments (complete response)
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent drafter must fully answer (respond to) all of the examiner’s comments on the application set out in the office action. If the patent drafter does not respond to all of the examiner’s rejections and does not rebut all of the points raised, the response is likely to be considered nonresponsive and the patent examiner will reject the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent drafter must always strive to file a complete response to an office action because not responding in full to the office action can seriously impair the client’s rights. Explain the draft response to the client; the client may help identify distinctions and choose among amendment options. Be proactive in rebutting examiner misunderstandings by drawing attention to additional information and documentation that offers evidence suggesting that the claims should be allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe time limits for responses to office actions (timeliness/docketing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the world’s patent offices impose time limits on the filing of responses to office actions. In a typical office action in the United States, for example, the applicant has three months in the former instance and another three months in the latter (totaling six months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand country-specific periods and whether the running date is the mailing date of the response or the date of the office action. Missing deadlines (or filing extremely close to them) can lead to abandonment because filing a response to a final office action does not itself suspend the deadline unless specific actions occur. Docket deadlines and client responsibilities for annuity/maintenance payments should be tracked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be proactive in rebuttal options to obviousness rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: When an examiner finds the claimed invention motivated to combine prior art references, the examiner will reject the pending claim for obviousness. The patent drafter can rebut such a rejection by: arguing the examiner has misunderstood cited prior art; arguing the examiner has misunderstood the applicant’s invention/pending claims; arguing the lack of inventive step cannot be asserted by combining the cited references; and/or amending the pending claims so they recite an invention not disclosed in or obvious from the cited prior art references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patent drafter must not be a passive actor. Counsel the client on rebuttal options and point to additional evidence that suggests allowance. Prepare arguments and, where appropriate, claim amendments to overcome cited references.

rubrics_metrics.name: No new matter: amendments must not introduce subject matter beyond original disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A universal rule in most jurisdictions is that no new matter (new subject matter) beyond that originally disclosed as of the filing date may be added (except to remedy obvious mistakes, such as typographic errors). The same rule applies in principle to both the claims and the description and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The restriction balances inventors’ rights and third-party predictability; therefore drafting a complete disclosure prior to filing is of paramount importance. If broad claims are not fully supported by the filed disclosure, you cannot add new embodiments later to justify breadth. Examiners generally allow clarifying language, prior art references, or resolving inconsistencies, but substantial additions risk being regarded as new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of original disclosure includes inherent or self-evident matter to skilled person
rubrics_metrics.description: The original disclosure covers not only matters explicitly described as of the filing date but also matters that a person skilled in the art would recognize as inherent to or self-evident from the original disclosure as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrating inherent disclosure requires more than mere possibility or probability; it requires that the information be necessarily present and a skilled person would readily recognize it. Example: specifying helical springs as a particular form of previously-disclosed 'resilient supports' may be new matter unless it is convincingly shown a person skilled in the art would naturally use helical springs in that context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional variation on what constitutes new matter (EPO standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: While many jurisdictions share common principles regarding permissible amendments, there are variations. In Europe, matters that are not 'directly and unambiguously derivable by those skilled in the art from the original disclosure' are assumed to be new matters that cannot be introduced after filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because EPO practice is strict, patent drafters often use extensive multiple dependent claims and explain all possible combinations of elements and features in the description as filed to maximize allowable amendment flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by reference can affect original disclosure (U.S. practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States, a reference to another patent literature in the description (incorporation by reference) could be part of the original disclosure and thus could be the basis for a later amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use caution and understand how cross-references may be treated as part of the original disclosure in different jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: When amending claims, check unity, consistency and support
rubrics_metrics.description: When amending the claims substantially and limiting their scope, examiners may pay particular attention to: (i) Do the amended claims satisfy the requirement of unity of invention? (ii) Will the amended claims be seriously inconsistent with the description, meaning that the description requires corresponding amendment? (iii) Conversely, are all amended claims supported by the description as filed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before filing claim amendments, evaluate these three questions. If the description does require amendment to avoid serious inconsistency, address that. Ensure support for all claim amendments in the originally filed disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modifying the stated problem/effect must be supported by the original disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon receipt of an office action raising lack of inventive step, a drafter may seek to restrict claims and revise the stated problem to emphasize a particular effect obtainable by the restricted invention that the cited prior art does not achieve. Such modification of the 'problem to be solved' is permissible only if that emphasized effect is supported by the original disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only emphasize effects that are deducible from the application as filed; otherwise the change may amount to new matter or unsupported amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative limitations and disclaimers raise new matter issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Amending claims by introducing a negative limitation (e.g., 'excluding X' or 'without performing Y') can raise issues of new matter if the excluded subject matter lacks support in the application as filed. For example, excluding a particular species not supported when only a genus was disclosed may introduce new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some jurisdictions permit certain disclaimers (e.g., to overcome accidental anticipation or to exclude nonpatentable subject matter), but this varies. Approach negative limitations through the lens of new matter and check jurisdictional rules carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadening claims during prosecution is limited and jurisdiction-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: In many jurisdictions, broadening the claim by removing claimed features is permissible during prosecution as long as no new matter is introduced. In Japan, amendment to claim a broader concept or to remove claimed features is not allowed unless such amendments do not add any new technical significance. In some jurisdictions (EPO, China), it is impermissible to delete from an independent claim a feature the application consistently presented as 'essential'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid characterizing features in the description as 'essential' or 'indispensable' unless needed, because that may prevent later deletion or broadening. Know national limits on broadening amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding new claims during prosecution allowed only if no new matter and subject to national rules
rubrics_metrics.description: In many jurisdictions, adding a new claim during prosecution is not prohibited provided no new matter is introduced. Some jurisdictions, however, have special rules limiting addition of claims after certain procedural events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Japan: after receiving the first office action, amendments that change the special technical feature are prohibited; after final office action, additions are limited to deletion, narrowing, correction, or clarification. United States: substantial amendments after final are limited to (i) deletion of a claim; (ii) amendments as requested or suggested by the examiner; or (iii) amendments that raise no new issue. Plan claim additions with jurisdictional constraints in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners may conduct supplemental searches after claim amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner considers it necessary, they may conduct a supplemental search for pertinent prior art, particularly where the applicant amended the claims, taking into account the prior art cited in the first office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments may trigger further prior art discovery and additional office actions if the examiner remains unconvinced. Claims are often assessed under a 'broadest reasonable interpretation' in view of the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use interviews with examiners strategically and document them
rubrics_metrics.description: Many patent offices allow patent drafters and inventors to speak with the patent examiner about the pending application (an interview). Because official business will be discussed, both parties may be required to submit complete and accurate written descriptions of the interview; these records typically become part of the file history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare thoroughly: review the office action and prior art, be ready to explain in clear, concise and persuasive language why the claims are patentable, prepare possible claim amendments to share, and consider bringing the inventor (where permitted) after pre-counseling. Note: examiners typically do not conduct interviews before issuing the first office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second and subsequent office actions: expect narrower issues but possible fees and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent examiner issues a second office action, the patent drafter will need to prepare and file another response. Any second and subsequent office actions should, hopefully, involve a narrower set of issues than the first. The process may repeat until allowance, rejection, or abandonment; some offices limit continuation of the cycle or impose additional fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond more quickly to later actions if prior art overlaps; weigh financial/administrative costs versus benefit of continued prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final office action: remedy, appeal, or abandon; special deadline consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A final office action will require that the application be remedied to the examiner’s satisfaction, appealed or abandoned. In the United States, filing a response to a final office action does not itself satisfy deadline requirements; only certain actions suspend the deadline: (i) examiner issuing a notice of allowance; (ii) examiner issuing a new, nonfinal office action; (iii) abandoning the application; (iv) filing a request for continued examination; or (v) filing a notice of appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that filing very late may result in abandonment because the examiner may not review the late reply before the final deadline. Consider RCEs, appeals, or continuation strategies if appropriate and timely. Track final-action deadlines closely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal procedures vary by jurisdiction; consider administrative and judicial routes
rubrics_metrics.description: Many patent offices provide some form of administrative appeal for decisions made by individual examiners; this may involve review by a board of administrative judges and may be further appealed to a court depending on national law. In the U.S., the drafter submits an appeal brief and may request an oral hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals typically involve fees and timing constraints. Counsel the client on business benefits and costs when deciding to appeal versus other routes (continuation, licensing, abandonment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisional, continuation and continuation-in-part applications: definitions and strategic uses
rubrics_metrics.description: A divisional application is 'divided' from a parent application and claims only part of the invention set out in the parent; it may retain the parent’s filing and priority dates. In the United States, a continuation application discloses and claims only subject matter disclosed in a parent application and retains the parent’s filing date. A continuation-in-part repeats substantial portions of the parent and adds matter not disclosed in the parent; parts disclosed in the parent get parent's priority date, added matter gets CIP's filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use divisionals to pursue withdrawn claims (e.g., after restriction requirements), continuations to pursue variants of claims while keeping parent filing date, and CIPs to claim improvements developed after filing but be aware of priority date limitations for added matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisional vs continuation distinctions and timing constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Divisional applications in many jurisdictions may be filed within specified time limits (varies by country); in some jurisdictions a divisional may be filed at any time until expiry of the appeal period. In the U.S., divisionals are appropriate for addressing restriction requirement-related claim withdrawals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know national rules and timing for filing divisionals; consider strategic use when claims are rejected or when continuing prosecution in a separate pending case is desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition proceedings: pre-grant and post-grant challenges and practitioner role
rubrics_metrics.description: Third parties may challenge a patent grant before a court or through administrative opposition mechanisms. In pre-grant opposition, the office publishes claims for public opposition; opposers must argue convincingly (e.g., that the examiner missed key prior art). Applicants may rebut; opposition may be heard by the examiner or a special panel, and outcomes can be appealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware some parties strategically use oppositions to delay or narrow competitors’ patents. Patent drafters typically prepare opposition documents and should counsel clients that a notice of intended grant does not ensure immediate issuance without further delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent issuance formalities and post-issuance maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the patent examiner issues a notice of allowance, the drafter handles issuance formalities and discusses continuation options with the client. A patent is often issued months after fees are paid and issuance may be delayed by opposition procedures. After issuance, the owner must pay periodic maintenance or annuity fees to keep the patent in force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is usually no way to speed up printing/issuance; docket and/or confirm responsibility for annuity payments with the client or a third-party payment service. Discuss strategic continuation filings prior to issuance if client desires ongoing pending applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare a complete disclosure at filing as paramount
rubrics_metrics.description: Drafting a complete disclosure of the invention prior to filing is of paramount importance because later amendments are constrained by what was originally disclosed and third-party predictability concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include sufficient detail, embodiments, and combinations so that future claim narrowing or selections are supported. Anticipate possible examiner rejections and provide material that could support later allowable claim sets.
